chapter: Sidemen, mixed bands, the Apollo and Lena Horne
title: Freedom in the band and why musicians sought him out
summary: Barnet says players found him because he allowed freedom, with no uniform inspections, as long as they could play.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: In going through all of the jazz history books there are an enormous number of major musicians who mentioned having played with Charlie Barnet. It is absolutely phenomenal. All of the really important stars and contributors to jazz who have been through your bands. You picked some very fine people.

Well, Pat, you know, to my own amazement, I had a tablet like you've got there, and made out my own list, and I was amazed. But I tell you, I think it isn't a question that I found them so much as they maybe found me, just as much as I found them, maybe moreso. Because we had a freedom of expression in our band that the Dorseys, neither one of them, didn't have, and certainly Benny Goodman didn't have it. I mean he was quite a taskmaster, and I always had

a, you know, like go ahead and do your own thing, whatever you want to do, but be able to play, that's all I ask of you. There was no fingernail inspection or shined shoes or -- I more or less, if they fit in with the way we they were doing, they stayed. If they didn't they left. But musicians, you know, they have a way of finding situations like that. They would hear about it. That's why I say, as many or more of them found me than I found them. And I was very fortunate that way, because I had a bunch of wonderful blowers in that band, all kinds, all kinds of instruments.
